name: Hypoglossal nerve (CN XII)
summary: A purely motor nerve to the tongue. From the hypoglossal nucleus beneath the floor of the fourth ventricle the fibers pass ventrally between the medial lemniscus and the inferior olive and emerge as rootlets in the preolivary sulcus, leave the skull through the hypoglossal canal and curve down and forward between the carotid and jugular vessels to enter the tongue, supplying all its intrinsic muscles and the genioglossus, hyoglossus and styloglossus (the palatoglossus belongs to the vagus). A lower motor neuron lesion wastes half the tongue and deviates it toward the weak side; because its intramedullary fibers run through the medial medulla it is part of the medial medullary syndrome, and skull base tumors, carotid dissection and neck surgery injure it peripherally.

anatomy.location: Nucleus in the dorsal paramedian medulla beneath the hypoglossal trigone → fibers ventrally through the medulla lateral to the medial lemniscus → rootlets in the preolivary sulcus between the pyramid and olive → hypoglossal canal in the occipital condyle → descends between the internal carotid artery and internal jugular vein, crosses the carotid bifurcation and the loop of the lingual artery, and enters the tongue above the hyoid.

function: Movement of the tongue for speech, chewing and swallowing: protrusion (genioglossus), retraction (styloglossus), depression (hyoglossus) and shape changes (intrinsic muscles).

bestView.label: hypoglossal nucleus in the paramedian dorsal medulla; fibers to the preolivary sulcus
hypoglossal canal in the occipital condyle

imaging.normalAppearance: The rootlets are seen leaving the preolivary sulcus on thin T2; the hypoglossal canal is assessed on skull base CT and contrast MRI. Denervation of half the tongue appears as fatty, atrophic hemitongue on T1 and CT, a sign that may reveal the lesion before the patient notices.

pathology.finding: Paramedian ventral medullary restriction with ipsilateral tongue weakness and contralateral hemiparesis.
Metastasis, chordoma, glomus tumor or schwannoma in the canal or condyle with denervation of the hemitongue.
Mural hematoma of the internal carotid near the skull base with an isolated twelfth nerve palsy.
Fatty replacement and shrinkage of one half of the tongue on CT or T1.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: Skull base MRI with contrast and CT; carotid imaging; DWI

lesionEffects.deficit: Tongue deviates toward the weak side on protrusion, with wasting and fasciculations
lesionEffects.mechanism: Lower motor neuron: nucleus, rootlets, canal or neck

lesionEffects.deficit: Tongue deviates away from a hemispheric lesion without wasting
lesionEffects.mechanism: Supranuclear corticobulbar lesion (genioglossus mainly contralateral input)

lesionEffects.deficit: Dysarthria for lingual consonants and difficulty moving food in the mouth
Bilateral wasting and fasciculations with a spastic component
lesionEffects.mechanism: Motor neuron disease (mixed bulbar and pseudobulbar)

examination: Inspect the tongue at rest in the mouth for atrophy and fasciculations (protruding the tongue causes false fasciculations)
Protrude the tongue: deviation is toward the weak side; push against the cheek
Check the palate, voice, sternocleidomastoid (jugular foramen) and the limbs (medial medulla)
pearls: Tongue to the weak side: with wasting it is the nerve or nucleus; without wasting it is the opposite hemisphere
An isolated twelfth nerve palsy is a skull base or carotid lesion until imaged: metastasis, chordoma, dissection

pitfalls: Fasciculations of the protruded tongue are normal; look at the tongue at rest

nuclei.component: GSE: intrinsic and extrinsic tongue muscles

exit.brainstemExit: Preolivary sulcus of the medulla between the pyramid and the olive, as 10–15 rootlets
exit.cisternalCourse: Cerebellomedullary cistern in front of the vertebral artery and PICA, converging on the hypoglossal canal
exit.foramen: Hypoglossal (anterior condylar) canal in the occipital condyle
exit.extracranialCourse: Between the internal carotid artery and internal jugular vein deep to the posterior belly of digastric, across the carotid bifurcation and the lingual artery, into the tongue above the hyoid

branches.name: Muscular branches
branches.supplies: genioglossus, hyoglossus, styloglossus, intrinsic muscles of the tongue

branches.name: Fibers from C1 travelling with the nerve
branches.supplies: geniohyoid and thyrohyoid; superior root of the ansa cervicalis (not truly hypoglossal)

tests.name: Inspection
tests.how: Tongue at rest in the floor of the mouth
tests.abnormal: Wasting, furrowing and fasciculations on the affected side (lower motor neuron)

tests.name: Lateral push
tests.how: Push the tongue into each cheek against your finger
tests.abnormal: Weak push toward the opposite side (the weak genioglossus cannot push across)

lesionSigns.sign: Unilateral wasting with contralateral hemiparesis and proprioceptive loss
Unilateral wasting with IX, X, XI palsies
lesionSigns.localisingValue: skull base (Collet–Sicard, hypoglossal canal and jugular foramen)
hypoglossal canal or upper neck: tumor, carotid dissection, surgery

cranial.nuclearVsPeripheral: Nuclear lesions are medial medullary and are accompanied by contralateral hemiparesis and lemniscal loss; the nucleus is also a favorite of motor neuron disease, where bilateral wasting and fasciculations are the rule. Peripheral lesions are isolated or come with the other lower cranial nerves at the skull base.
cranial.supranuclear: The genioglossus receives mainly contralateral corticobulbar input, so a hemispheric stroke deviates the tongue toward the hemiparetic side (away from the lesion), without wasting; bilateral lesions make the tongue small, stiff and slow (pseudobulbar).
